fr:title.text: Spectral sequence of a tower of fibrations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spectral sequence of a tower of fibrations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a tower of maps X_n \to \cdots \to X_1 \to X_0 = 1, where we assume finite n for simplicity, we wish to compute the homotopy groups of X = X_n from the knowledge of the homotopy groups of the fibers F_n = \operatorname {fib}(X_n \to X_{n-1}).

For each fiber sequence F_n \to X_n \to X_{n-1}, there is a long exact sequence of homotopy groups, and we wish to arrange these information suitably so that knowing \pi _n (F_p) allows us to piece together \pi _n (X). This can be achieved using spectral sequences. See this link for another exposition.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The main difficulty of analyzing the situation is that \pi _n (F_p) is split into two parts that gets appropriated into \pi _{n} (X_p) and \pi _{n-1} (X_{p-1}). This gives multiple possibilities. The case would be easier if, in the rolled-up long exact sequence, one edge of the triangle is always zero. Then the exact sequence splits into various short exact sequences. Since F_p is a fiber, the natural direction is for j to be zero, implying i is epi and k is mono.

To do this, we consider collapsing i to its image, i.e. consider turing i into i' : i (\pi _n (X_p)) \to i (\pi _n (X_{p-1})), repeatedly. From one angle, this makes i iteratively more surjective. From another angle, in the limit, if we consider X_p = X_n where p \ge n, and X_p = 1 where p \le 0 (so F_p = 1 for out-of-bounds indices), then the maps eventually become \operatorname {im}(\pi _n(X) \to \pi _n(X_p)) \to \operatorname {im}(\pi _n(X) \to \pi _n(X_{p-1})), which are surjective. If we still have long exact sequences for these maps, then this produces a filtration F^p \pi _n (X) = \ker (\pi _n (X) \to \pi _n (X_p)) whose associated graded is known.

We have constructed a sequence of exact triangles such that for large enough r, they split into short exact sequences. So now the goal is to give a tractible way to compute the object E_{n,p,r} = \frac {k^{-1} \operatorname {im}(i^r : \pi _n (X_{p+r}) \to \pi _n (X_p))}{j \ker (i^r : \pi _{n-1} (X_{p+r-1}) \to \pi _{n-1} (X_{p-1}))}. As a sanity check, E_{n, p, 0} = \pi _n (F_p), being the “initial condition” for our sequence. Note that this is also the only data we have, as \pi _n (X_p) are all unknown. Therefore we want some way to compute E_{n,p,r+1} from the data of E_{n,p,r}. (As is the case for all spectral sequences, the “computation” relies on knowing some differentials, but they are often unique by formal reasons.)

Summarizing with the indices aligned with convention, given a tower of maps X = X_n \to \cdots \to X_1 \to X_0 = 1 between simply connected spaces, we have a spectral sequence E^2_{p,q} = \pi _{p+q} (F_q) \Rightarrow \pi _{p+q} (X). With some more work, we can deal with infinite towers and non-simply connected spaces, with sufficiently nice hypotheses.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: On a computer, you can press Ctrl–K to search for trees.
I try to adhere to several principles when composing trees.

html:ul.html:li: If a definition or a lemma would present itself during a proof attempt, then do not introduce it until that part of the proof. The nature of forests makes this kind of organization more viable, as each definition is a tree by itself.
If a part of a proof has an easy constructive phrasing, use it and avoid classical reasoning. But if it requires some complication, then the classical way is used.

Avoid abstraction leaks. Even if A is defined as B, do not use them interchangeably. For instance, an ideal is defined as a subset of a ring satisfying certain conditions. But we will insist on writing ideals as numbers, for example saying \mathfrak {a} \mid x instead of x \in \mathfrak {a}. This is not too heretic, since algebraic number theory already uses this kind of notation. Similarly, although prime ideals correspond to points in \operatorname {Spec}(A), we do not identify them.
Apply unbiased terminology and negative thinking.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A short exact sequence is an exact sequence with all but three consecutive terms being zero. It is often written as 0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0. The short exact sequence describes how B is made up of a subobject A and a quotient C.
